```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
```

A simulation study is an experiment on statistical methods. Data are drawn
from a known mechanism, each method is applied to each data set, and the
results are compared with the known truth. The design of such a study is
usually described with the ADEMP structure of Morris, White and Crowther
(2019): **A**ims, **D**ata-generating mechanisms, **E**stimands,
**M**ethods and **P**erformance measures.

adempR turns that structure into code. Each part of a study is a declared
object, the run is recorded in a directory that can be stopped and resumed,
every replication can be replayed, and every performance measure comes with
its Monte Carlo standard error and its own denominator. This vignette walks
through one complete study.

```{r}
library(adempR)
```

## Aims and data-generating mechanisms

We want to know how well the one sample t interval covers a normal mean in
small samples, and how often the t test rejects. The data-generating
mechanisms are normal samples of size 10 or 40, with mean 0 or 0.5.

```{r}
scenarios <- sim_scenarios(n = c(10L, 40L), mu = c(0, 0.5), sigma = 1)
scenarios
```

Each scenario has a key computed from its values, not from its position.
Reordering the factors or their levels gives the same keys, and therefore
the same random numbers.

The generator receives one scenario and a context, and returns a data set.
It must use only R's random number generator, which adempR seeds for it.

```{r}
generate <- function(scenario, context) {
  data.frame(y = rnorm(scenario$n, scenario$mu, scenario$sigma))
}
```

## Estimands

An estimand is the quantity a method should estimate, defined independently
of any method. Here it is the population mean, and its true value is known
exactly in each scenario.

```{r}
mean_estimand <- sim_estimand(
  "mean", population = "normal DGP", effect = "marginal", scale = "identity",
  truth = sim_truth_exact(function(scenario) scenario$mu))
```

When the truth is not available in closed form, use
`sim_truth_numeric()` or `sim_truth_mc()`; see
`vignette("estimands-and-truth")`.

## Methods

A method takes the data (and, if it declares them, some scenario fields) and
returns one `sim_estimate()` per estimand. The estimate, its standard
error, its interval and its test are reported separately, because each can
be valid or invalid on its own.

```{r}
t_method <- function(data) {
  fit <- t.test(data$y, mu = 0)
  sim_estimate("mean", estimate = mean(data$y),
               se = sd(data$y) / sqrt(nrow(data)),
               lower = fit$conf.int[1], upper = fit$conf.int[2], level = 0.95,
               p_value = fit$p.value, null = 0)
}
wald_method <- function(data) {
  m <- mean(data$y)
  se <- sd(data$y) / sqrt(nrow(data))
  sim_estimate("mean", estimate = m, se = se,
               lower = m - 1.96 * se, upper = m + 1.96 * se, level = 0.95,
               p_value = 2 * pnorm(-abs(m / se)), null = 0)
}
```

## The study

`sim_study()` combines the parts with the performance measures and a
protocol. `sim_validate()` checks the declarations and, with
`smoke = TRUE`, runs one replication per scenario.

```{r}
study <- sim_study(
  name = "normal_mean",
  aims = "Coverage and rejection of t and Wald intervals for a normal mean",
  scenarios = scenarios,
  generate = generate,
  estimands = list(mean_estimand),
  methods = list(t = t_method, wald = wald_method),
  measures = c("bias", "empse", "mean_se", "coverage", "width", "rejection"),
  protocol = sim_protocol(purpose = "exploratory",
                          precision_targets = c(coverage = 0.01)))
sim_validate(study, smoke = TRUE)
```

## Planning the number of replications

The coverage MCSE is about `sqrt(p (1 - p) / R)`. To estimate coverage near
0.95 with an MCSE of 0.01 we need

```{r}
sim_plan_replications("proportion", p = 0.95, mcse = 0.01)
```

replications per scenario. We use 500 here to keep the vignette fast.

## Running

A run lives in a directory. Chunks of replications are committed
atomically, so an interrupted run can be resumed by calling `sim_run()`
again with the same arguments.

```{r}
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "normal-mean-run")
run <- sim_run(study, replications = 500, seed = 2026, path = path)
run
```

## Performance

```{r}
perf <- sim_summarise(run)
perf
```

Each row reports the value, its Monte Carlo standard error, an interval,
and the number of replications that were eligible for that measure. The
rejection rate is labeled as the type I error when the null is true
(`mu = 0`) and as power otherwise.

```{r}
s <- as.data.frame(perf)
s[s$measure == "coverage", c("scenario_id", "method", "value", "mcse", "n_eligible")]
```

The Wald interval undercovers when `n = 10` because it ignores the
uncertainty in the standard deviation. The paired comparison uses the
same data sets for both methods, so its MCSE is much smaller than the two
separate MCSEs would suggest.

```{r}
sim_compare(run, c("t", "wald"), measures = c("coverage", "width"))
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Coverage of the t and Wald intervals with Monte Carlo intervals"}
sim_plot(run, "precision", measure = "coverage")
```

## Replay and report

Any replication can be recomputed from the run directory. The replay uses
the recorded random number streams and checks that the results match.

```{r}
rp <- sim_replay(run, scenario = 1, replication = 17)
rp$matches
```

`sim_report()` writes a self-contained HTML report, and `sim_export()`
writes a bundle with tables, code, checksums and a reanalysis script.

```{r}
report <- file.path(tempdir(), "normal-mean.html")
sim_report(run, report, overwrite = TRUE)
file.exists(report)
```
